title: 2027 Triumph Tiger 1200 Aims For The BMW GS's Do-Everything Crown - Jalopnik
content: If you want a motorcycle that does everything, you buy a BMW GS. It's such an easy choice, so rote that even BMW itself has felt the need to specialize its adventure lineup away from such perfectly omnicapable bikes. Now, though, another brand thinks it can hit the Bavarians where their hold is strongest. Triumph has revamped the Tiger 1200 lineup to hit BMW where it hurts, and the Brits have a solid shot of making a real mark. The Tiger 1200 line is still split into its four component models — GT Pro, Rally Pro, GT Explorer, and Rally Explorer — but Triumph has streamlined things between the four bikes to make their differences clearer. Every model now comes with a 19 inch front wheel and a 17 out back, and all four get trick self-lowering Showa suspension with 7.9 inches of travel front and rear — until you come to a stop, at which point the system drops the bike almost 1.2 inches. Triumph says the seat height, with a low seat installed and the self-lowering suspension active, can get as low as 31.1 inches at a stop. That's impressively low for a big adventure bike, and over an inch shorter than the competing R 1300 GS. On top of the trick suspension updates, Triumph has updated the Tiger's rider display — a new 7-inch display with Apple CarPlay and Android Auto now standard. There's also the updated 1,160cc three-cylinder engine with a redesigned cylinder head, new pistons, lighter intake and exhaust valves, and revised gear ratios for first, second, and third. The engine now makes 155.8 horsepower (up from 147 hp). Triumph also claims that the new Tiger 1200 has more torque down low, which improves slow-speed performance. If you're a bit confused by all the Tiger 1200's available variants, here's how Triumph differentiates them: GT bikes get cast wheels, while the Rally bikes get spokes. Rally bikes get an extra off-road ride mode and some engine protection. Explorer bikes get wider and taller handlebars and 7.9-gallon fuel tanks rather than the Pro bikes' 5.3-gallon units. Got all that? Essentially, they're the same chassis, engine, and suspension across all models, but the Rally bikes get some dirt features, and Explorer bikes get the right gear for long tours. All four get Bosch radar front and rear, as well, to enable both adaptive cruise control and rear close-follow warnings — they're all competent tourers, big tank or no. The best change for 2027 to my eye, though, is the appearance of the new Tiger 1200 lineup. The prior bikes were stuck in an awkward in-between period, where Triumph was in the process of ditching its long-lasting twin-headlight design but hadn't yet gone all-in on compact LED illumination. Now it has, and the Tiger looks all the better for it — that single center headlight below the light bar really works for me. It's functional, too, with corner lighting built into the central LED that illuminates when the rider leans.

title: GS Entec's Ulsan Plant: Asia's Largest Offshore Wind Hub - 조선일보
content: 300 Billion Won Facility Automates Monopile Production for 15MW Turbines, Secures Major Contracts GS Group is accelerating its expansion into the eco-friendly energy ecosystem. The company has transformed GS Entec, which previously manufactured large-scale equipment for GS Caltex and other petrochemical plants, into Asia’s largest production hub for offshore wind turbine foundations. GS Entec held a completion ceremony on October 26 at its Ulsan Yongjam Plant for a 300 billion Korean won automated production facility dedicated to monopiles. Monopiles are massive steel pillars driven into the seabed to support offshore wind turbines. The event was attended by GS Group Chairman Huh Tae-soo, GS Co., Ltd. Vice Chairman Hong Soon-ki, GS Entec CEO Huh Chul-hong, and Koen Bogers, CEO of Dutch partner Sif. Chairman Huh has shown particular interest in the business transition, reportedly visiting the site multiple times to monitor progress. GS Entec has long produced ultra-large chemical equipment, including pressure vessels and heat exchangers for petrochemical plants. However, as global carbon neutrality efforts slowed traditional petrochemical plant orders, the company had to revise its survival strategy. GS Group and GS Entec found a solution in technological continuity: the precision machining and welding of thick steel plates required for petrochemical pressure vessels closely resemble the processes needed for monopile production. Partnering with Sif, the world’s top monopile manufacturer, GS Entec began overhauling its Ulsan factory in October 2024, automating key processes. With an annual production capacity of 150,000 tons, the facility is Asia’s first and largest capable of producing monopiles for 15MW-class offshore wind turbines. It has already secured contracts to supply 64 monopiles worth 200 billion Korean won for the Yeonggwang Nakwol Offshore Wind Project (365MW) and 37 large monopiles for the Taean Offshore Wind Project. Leveraging this track record, GS Entec plans to aggressively target markets in Japan and other parts of Asia.

title: Stablecoin Firm RedotPay To Hold IPO By Year’s End: Reports - The Globe and Mail
content: Multiple media reports say that Hong Kong-based stablecoin firm RedotPay plans to hold a U.S. initial public offering (IPO) by year's end. According to the reports, RedotPay is planning to make a confidential regulatory filing to hold its IPO before the end of 2026 at a potential valuation of $5 billion U.S. A confidential filing would allow U.S. regulators to review draft offering documents before the company makes its registration statement publicly available. Wall Street banks JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: $JPM) and Goldman Sachs (NYSE: $GS) are reportedly advising on the proposed share sale. However, RedotPay has not announced a listing venue, share price, offering size, or expected trading date for its stock. RedotPay had planned to hold its IPO earlier this year but canceled those plans amid an ongoing legal dispute involving crypto exchange Binance. In the lawsuit, Binance and its affiliates are seeking $473 million U.S. in damages from RedotPay. The lawsuit claims that confidential business information helped RedotPay develop a competing payments service and steal Binance customers. Specifically, Binance claims that more than 470,000 former Binance Card customers have moved to RedotPay. The legal dispute remains ongoing. The lawsuit does not appear to be deterring RedotPay from its plans to go public this year. Founded in 2023, RedotPay provides cryptocurrency payment cards, multicurrency wallets, and global transfer services, with stablecoins forming a big part of its business. The company reportedly serves more than nine million customers and employs approximately 280 people worldwide. RedotPay most recently reported that its annualized revenue surpassed $180 million U.S. The firm raised $194 million U.S. in a 2025 funding round. © Copyright 2026 The Globe and Mail Inc. title: GS Entec pivots to offshore wind, invests 300b won to expand Korea capacity - Chosunbiz
content: Ulsan plant overhaul quadruples monopile output as GS Entec eyes Japanese orders and seeks stronger port backing A cylindrical steel structure "can" with a diameter of 10 m and a thickness of 90 mm was neatly placed on advanced automated production equipment. Welders poured dozens of steady sparks from two points inside and four outside. The precise welding work to join giant steel plates was being carried out without human hands. After repeatedly welding along the circumference of a "section" formed by joining cans, a 10-step process of coating and shipping meshed like an organism within a 250,000㎡ site. ◇ Dedicated monopile plant after 2 years…production capacity expanded by about fourfold The "dedicated monopile production facility completion ceremony" held on the 26th at GS Entec's Ulsan Yongjam Plant was not merely an event to announce the completion of facilities. GS Group Chairman Huh Tae-soo said it "is meaningful" in that the company seized the era's shift to energy transition as a new business opportunity and achieved a proactive business pivot. Technical cooperation partner Sif CEO Coon Voghers of the Netherlands also said it is "a starting point" for GS Entec to continuously contribute to the energy transition on which future generations' lives depend. A monopile is a cylindrical steel structure that supports an offshore wind turbine from the seabed. Until just two years ago, this plant produced refining and petrochemical equipment. But as the petrochemical industry suffered from oversupply and the offshore wind market expanded with countries' carbon neutrality policies, GS Entec also had to find a new growth engine. That is why GS Entec decided in Jul. 2024 to invest 300 billion won to convert its production facilities. It was a choice to change the very constitution of the company, beyond simply switching product lines. With this conversion, GS Entec greatly increased its annual monopile production capacity from 40,000 tons to 150,000 tons. It can manufacture ultra-large monopiles with a maximum diameter of 11 m, steel plate thickness of 160 mm, length of 100 m, and weight of 2,500 tons. It also produces products used in 15 MW-class large offshore wind turbines. It applied steel plate processing and welding technologies accumulated in the refining and petrochemical equipment manufacturing process to the offshore wind sector and built automated facilities to improve production efficiency. ◇ After Yeonggwang-Nakwol, wins 37 units for Taean, targets Japan market Orders are piling up. In the Jeonnam Yeonggwang-Nakwol offshore wind project, GS Entec won an order for 64 monopiles worth about 200 billion won and completed installation by Jun. this year. Last month, it signed a contract to supply 37 monopiles for the 504 MW Taean Offshore Wind project to be built off the coast of Taean, South Chungcheong. The supply volume is 51,000 tons, about 34% of annual production capacity. Deliveries will be made sequentially from Jul. next year to Aug. 2028. GS Entec plans to expand its sales channels from domestic offshore wind projects to overseas markets, including Japan, Asia, and Australia. Park Ki-yeol, GS Entec's sales and order management team leader, said, "We are aiming to win two to three projects in Korea and one to two in Japan." In particular, it plans to expand orders in line with capacity, focusing on nine projects expected to be tendered from mid-2028 to 2030. ◇ Tasks in port infrastructure amid low-priced push from China…government support is key The key is government support for industrial infrastructure. Japan has designated seven hub ports that support assembly and installation of offshore wind equipment and is refurbishing the piers. The United Kingdom also said in Jan. this year that it had induced 3.4 billion pounds (about 6 trillion won) in private investment by injecting 204 million pounds (about 360 billion won) in public funds into manufacturing facilities and ports. China's price offensive is also fierce. According to energy market research firm Rystad Energy, China's monopile manufacturing cost is about 41% lower than Europe's. Price competition pressure is growing on our corporations as well. Domestically, securing port infrastructure is cited as a task no less important than production facilities. Co-CEO Song Won-gil of GS Entec said, "Because of offshore weather conditions, the number of days when actual monopile installation work is possible is about 90 days a year," and noted, "We need a dedicated logistics hub that can store pre-made monopiles and supply them immediately when conditions allow installation." The ground bearing capacity of general piers is about 5 tons per ㎡, but to handle ultra-large monopiles, they must withstand 30 tons or more per ㎡. GS Entec is currently utilizing existing facilities such as Mokpo New Port, Mokpo Daebul Industrial Complex, and Ulsan Port. There is no immediate disruption to production, but the position is that a separate logistics base is needed to store and transport large volumes stably. CEO Song said, "If the government takes the lead in preparing related facilities, corporations can also participate in funds or endowments and make use of them." In Jul., the government announced a plan to expand eight berths for offshore wind support piers at five ports—Mokpo, Gunsan, Incheon, Ulsan, and Taean. However, as they are being pursued for various purposes such as assembly, installation, and maintenance of power generation equipment, it is unclear whether they will meet the shipping demand of monopile manufacturers. Observers say that for the expansion of production facilities to translate into export competitiveness, port support that takes into account conditions for storing and loading ultra-large equipment is needed. In practice, tasks such as consultations among relevant ministries and compensation for fishing rights remain before pier expansion can proceed. An official of the National Assembly's Committee on Climate, Energy, Environment and Labor said, "The expansion of offshore wind support piers is not a matter decided by an announcement from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries alone, and requires consultations with local governments and the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment," and added, "Because there are compensation issues for fishing rights and customary fishing, we will consult at the standing committee level to ensure local governments push ahead with commitment." A key government official also said, "As the president has stressed that 'the nation's fate depends on the transition of the energy system,' this is a task that must move faster," and noted, "Consultations are currently underway among relevant ministries." title: GS Entec Transforms Ulsan Factory into Offshore Wind Base - 조선일보
content: Investing 300 Billion Won, GS Entec Automates Monopile Production for 15MW Turbines with Sif GS Entec, which has produced equipment for oil refining and petrochemical plants, has invested 300 billion Korean won to transform its Ulsan factory into a specialized production base for offshore wind turbine substructures. Leveraging its 30 years of accumulated technology in manufacturing large-scale steel equipment, the company has made a leap from the traditional 'smokestack industry' to the eco-friendly energy sector. On October 26, GS Entec held a completion ceremony for its 'Monopile (Monopile) dedicated automated production facility' at its Yongjam factory in Ulsan. The event was attended by Huh Tae-soo, GS Group chairman; Hong Soon-ki, GS vice chairman; Huh Chul-hong, CEO of GS Entec; and Koen Bogers, CEO of Dutch company Sif, among others. A monopile is a massive steel pillar driven into the seabed to support offshore wind turbines. GS Entec partnered with Sif, the world's top monopile manufacturer, and began a full-scale renovation of its Ulsan factory in October 2024, automating many core processes. With an annual production capacity of 150,000 tons, the facility is Asia's first and largest capable of producing monopiles to support ultra-large wind turbines rated at 15MW (megawatts). Huh Tae-soo, GS Group chairman, stated, "The completion of this facility, which transformed a chemical equipment factory into a renewable energy production site, is a symbolic example of seizing energy transition as a new business opportunity." He added, "It demonstrates GS Group's expansion into future growth areas such as AI data centers and renewable energy infrastructure." It was reported that Chairman Huh paid special attention to the factory conversion, visiting the site multiple times during the process. ◇ Factory that made chemical equipment for 30 years switches to offshore wind power Established in 1988, GS Entec is a subsidiary of GS Global. The company has achieved stable performance by manufacturing large-scale chemical equipment, including pressure vessels and reactors for oil refining and petrochemical plants. However, as global carbon neutrality trends slowed orders for traditional oil refining and petrochemical plants, revising its survival strategy became inevitable. GS Group and GS Entec found the answer in technological continuity. They recognized that the technology for manufacturing pressure vessels for oil refineries and monopiles shares similarities in precisely processing and welding thick steel plates. As offshore wind turbines have grown larger, reaching 10-15MW, monopiles are also trending toward larger diameters and heavier weights. The companies believed that leveraging GS Entec's steel manufacturing technology would secure competitiveness. During a visit on October 26, the Yongjam factory in Ulsan was in the process of trial-producing monopiles. The expansive factory, covering a total site area of 250,000 square meters, was designed to allow massive steel plates and processed components to move along the production line via conveyor belts, large grippers, and lifts. To create a monopile, steel plates weighing approximately 20 tons each are first welded together to form a 30-meter-long plate. The edges are then precision-finished to within ±0.5mm tolerance. The plate is rolled into a cylindrical shape using a large bending machine. Welding the ends of the rolled plate creates a massive ring-shaped 'can.' The factory can produce cans with a diameter of 11 meters and a steel plate thickness of 160mm. Multiple cans are precisely welded together to form a steel pillar for offshore wind turbines, measuring 100 meters in length and weighing 2,500 tons. The automation of key processes—from steel plate processing to cylindrical forming, welding, and assembly—is a hallmark of the Yongjam factory. Order achievements are already emerging. Before the factory conversion, in 2023, GS Entec secured an order worth approximately 200 billion Korean won for 64 monopiles measuring 7.5 meters in diameter and 71 meters in length for the Yeonggwang Nakwol Offshore Wind Project, 365MW, completing installation last June. In September, the company additionally won a contract to supply 37 monopiles for the Taean Offshore Wind Project, 504MW. These are large products with a diameter of approximately 10.6 meters and a length of approximately 80 meters. The offshore wind market is also expected to expand. The government announced a mid- to long-term bidding roadmap for offshore wind in June, planning to put a total of 55GW-scale projects up for competitive bidding over 10 years until 2035. GS Entec plans to use its domestic order achievements as a foothold to target the Asian market, including Japan.

Song Won-gil, CEO of GS Entec, made the remarks Monday at a press conference marking the completion of the company's dedicated monopile production facility at its Yongjam factory in Ulsan. GS Entec is the only company in South Korea that manufactures cylindrical offshore wind substructures known as monopiles. GS Entec's core business was once large-scale chemical plants, but the company has been pivoting since 2022, when it began a partnership with Sif, the world's leading offshore wind substructure manufacturer based in the Netherlands. The newly completed monopile facility was built by retrofitting existing chemical plant equipment with automated systems, at a total cost of 300 billion won ($227 million). A dedicated port capable of bearing the weight of offshore wind turbine components — each weighing thousands of tons — has long been an industry priority. Standard ports cannot handle such loads, making it difficult to stockpile large quantities of equipment. The monopiles GS Entec recently supplied for the Yeonggwang Nakwol project, for instance, weigh 880 tons each, while a typical port berth can support only about 3 tons per square meter. "Given South Korea's offshore weather conditions, there are only 90 days a year when construction work on an offshore wind complex is possible," Song said. "We need a port near the complex where equipment can be stored and deployed immediately on days when installation is feasible." He added that a port along the south or west coast — where most offshore wind turbines are installed — would help ensure continuity of operations. Song also raised the need to build infrastructure capable of meeting government procurement volumes. "With the government pushing hard on offshore wind policy, ports and other infrastructure must be expanded in tandem to keep pace with the volume of orders that will come out every year," he said. The government is targeting 25 GW of offshore wind capacity by 2035, adding 4 GW per year. Meeting that pace will require expanded port infrastructure to ensure timely delivery of components to newly developed offshore wind complexes each year. The completion ceremony at the Yongjam factory on Monday was attended by GS Group Chairman Heo Tae-soo, GS Entec CEO Heo Cheol-hong and Sif CEO Koen Bogers. GS Entec began building the facility in 2024 and finished construction two years later. The completion brings GS Entec's annual monopile production capacity from 40,000 tons to 150,000 tons, making it Asia's first facility dedicated exclusively to manufacturing extra-large monopiles. Since entering the monopile market in 2022, GS Entec has consistently built up its domestic track record. In 2023, it supplied 64 monopiles worth around 200 billion won for the Yeonggwang Nakwol offshore wind project, and in September it signed a contract to supply 37 monopiles for the Taean wind power project. The company plans to pursue overseas contracts as well, starting with Japan. "We will bid on all three projects scheduled in Japan after 2028," Song said, adding that the Taean wind power project would serve as a key reference for winning Japanese contracts. GS Group Chairman Heo Tae-soo, who attended the ceremony, said the completion of the Yongjam factory carried symbolic significance as it transformed a legacy chemical equipment facility into a renewable energy infrastructure site — turning the energy transition into a concrete business opportunity through an active strategic pivot. He said the project demonstrated that GS Group is broadening its business scope by seeking new opportunities in future growth sectors, including AI data centers, renewable energy and related infrastructure. In his welcoming remarks, GS Entec CEO Heo Cheol-hong said the company would combine Sif's technological expertise with GS Entec's manufacturing capabilities to strengthen quality and delivery competitiveness, and expand its presence in the global offshore wind market on the strength of its domestic track record.

content: The 2024 BMW R 1300 GS is a ground-up redesign of the flagship adventure bike, built around a new boxer twin in a slimmer, lighter package. It is designed to tour in comfort, carve mountain roads, and keep going when the pavement ends. The 1300cc horizontally opposed twin is more oversquare than the 1254cc engine it replaces, with a 13.3:1 compression ratio and ShiftCam variable valve timing. Peak output climbs to 145 horsepower, and the powerband is broad, with strong pull from the midrange to the 9000 rpm redline. Cooling is a mix of liquid and air, and final drive is by shaft. BMW moved the 6-speed transmission beneath the engine rather than behind it. That shortens the engine, makes room for a longer swingarm, and helps cut 26 pounds from the GS, which has a 523-pound curb weight. The wet multiplate clutch has a slipper function and hydraulic actuation, and a quickshifter is optional. The chassis is new, too. A steel sheet-metal main frame uses the engine as a stressed member, and the bolt-on cast-aluminum subframe can be replaced if damaged. The redesigned Evo Telelever front end eliminates the flex of earlier versions for more precise steering and clearer front-end feedback, while the Evo Paralever swingarm is longer and stiffer. Fully linked brakes use 310mm front discs with radially mounted 4-piston calipers. Standard equipment includes Road, Rain, Eco, and Enduro ride modes, a 6.5-inch TFT display, heated grips, keyless ride, tire pressure monitoring, hill-hold control, a Matrix LED headlight, and Metzeler Karoo 4 tires. Options include three more ride modes, semi-active suspension, adaptive ride height that lowers the seat 1.2 inches at low speeds, and radar-based Active Cruise Control. Beyond the base model, the R 1300 GS comes in Triple Black, GS Trophy, and Option 719 Tramuntana variants, each with its own finishes, seats, and equipment. Premium, Comfort, and Enduro Pro packages bundle popular options, and seven seat combinations allow seat heights from 31.5 to 35 inches. title: Goldman or Morgan Stanley: Which Stock Is Better Bet Post Q3 Results? - The Globe and Mail
content: Wall Street heavyweights The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc.GS and Morgan StanleyMS continue to capitalize on improving investment banking (IB) activity, robust equities trading and growing demand for financial services. Both companies delivered impressive third-quarter 2026 results, reflecting their strong market positions and ability to navigate a dynamic operating environment. The continued recovery in mergers and acquisitions (M&As), healthy underwriting activity, and strong institutional client engagement have supported their financial performances. While Goldman has demonstrated stronger IB revenue growth and trading momentum, Morgan Stanley continues to benefit from its diversified business model and expanding wealth management franchise. Against this backdrop, which IB powerhouse offers better investment prospects following the latest quarterly results? Let us examine. Goldman remains a dominant player in M&A advisory, underwriting and trading. The company's IB business has benefited significantly from improving global dealmaking activity and capital markets issuance. During the first nine months of 2026, IB fees jumped 40% year over year to $9.46 billion, supported by increases of 34%, 73% and 29% in advisory, equity underwriting and debt underwriting revenues, respectively. Management continues to view the capital markets environment favorably, with opportunities arising from strategic dealmaking, technology investments and AI infrastructure financing. Although higher interest rates and macroeconomic uncertainties could affect deal activity, GS's leading market position and healthy pipeline position it well to capitalize on the ongoing investment banking recovery. Goldman continues to streamline its operations by exiting non-core consumer banking businesses and strengthening its core franchises. The company is accelerating expansion in asset and wealth management to diversify its revenue sources and generate more durable fee-based income. In sync with these efforts, in August 2026, Goldman announced an agreement to acquire NEOS Investments, a provider of derivative income exchange-traded funds (ETFs). In April 2026, Goldman completed the acquisition of Innovator Capital Management, expanding its active exchange-traded fund (ETF) capabilities. Earlier, it completed the acquisition of Industry Ventures to strengthen its presence in venture capital and alternative investments. These initiatives complement its efforts to expand private market offerings and deepen client relationships. The benefits of Goldman's strategic repositioning are increasingly evident in its financial performance. For the first nine months of 2026, GBM revenues jumped 34% to $41.72 billion, while AWM revenues rose 15% to $13.73 billion. Continued asset gathering and strategic acquisitions should support recurring fee income and reduce the dependence on market-sensitive businesses over time. Morgan Stanley continues to leverage its integrated business model, encompassing institutional securities, wealth management and investment management. The company has strategically diversified its revenue streams to reduce the dependence on volatile capital markets activities while benefiting from improving IB conditions. The company's IB performance remained strong during the first nine months of 2026, with consolidated IB revenues increasing 30% year over year to $7.30 billion. The company is well-positioned to benefit from a healthier deal environment, supported by a robust and diversified pipeline across regions and sectors. Momentum is expanding beyond the Americas into Asia and EMEA, while active M&A and IPO markets, together with the company’s strong competitive position, are expected to support further growth as the macroeconomic backdrop evolves. Morgan Stanley's strategic focus on expanding wealth and investment management operations remains a major strength. Acquisitions such as E*TRADE and Eaton Vance have enhanced its scale and diversified its business mix. Further, the acquisition of EquityZen, completed in January 2026, strengthened its private markets capabilities and offerings for corporate and wealth management clients. The benefits of this transformation were evident in the first nine months of 2026. Wealth Management revenues increased 13.4% year over year to $26.44 billion. Moreover, the business attracted $498.9 billion in net new assets and $173.3 billion in fee-based asset flows during the first nine months of 2026. Wealth Management client assets reached $8.43 trillion as of September-end, up 19.5% year over year, while combined client assets across Wealth and Investment Management stood at $10.5 trillion, highlighting the growing scale of Morgan Stanley's wealth management franchise. This expanding client asset base provides Morgan Stanley with significant opportunities to generate recurring fee revenues and deepen client engagement. Over the past year, Goldman shares have gained 10.9%, outperforming Morgan Stanley’s 8.1% rise. In comparison, the industry has returned 3.3%. From a valuation perspective, Goldman appears relatively attractive. Its forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio stands at 11.94X, below Morgan Stanley's 13.56X. The valuation discount suggests that Goldman offers a relatively attractive entry point, particularly given its stronger recent earnings growth. In terms of shareholder returns, both companies continue to prioritize dividends and share repurchases. Following the Federal Reserve's 2026 stress test, GS increased its quarterly common stock dividend 11% to $5 per share. Similarly, in July, the company increased its quarterly dividend 15% to $1.15 per share. Morgan Stanley offers a dividend yield of 2.56% compared with Goldman's 2.28%. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for GS’ 2026 and 2027 earnings indicate 38.1% and 4.3% growth, respectively. Earnings estimates for both years have been revised upward over the past month. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for MS’ 2026 and 2027 earnings indicate 25.7% and 3.9% growth, respectively. Earnings estimates for both years have been revised upward over the past month. Both Goldman and Morgan Stanley remain well-positioned to benefit from the recovery in investment banking activity and growing demand for asset and wealth management services. Goldman's strong IB franchise, solid equities trading performance and strategic initiatives to expand its asset and wealth management operations should continue to support earnings growth. Its attractive valuation relative to Morgan Stanley offers a potential margin of safety, although elevated expenses and capital markets volatility remain concerning. Morgan Stanley, by contrast, offers greater earnings diversification, supported by its expanding wealth management franchise, recurring fee income and strong client asset inflows. Its superior dividend yield and solid capital position make it an attractive option for investors seeking a combination of growth and shareholder returns. However, its relatively expensive valuation could limit near-term upside. Overall, Goldman appears to be the more compelling investment choice at current levels. Its stronger earnings momentum, greater exposure to recovering investment banking activity and relatively favorable valuation position it for potentially higher returns. title: Longview business works with outreach mission to give bikes to employed people in need - Longview News-Journal
content: A partnership between a Longview shop and a homeless outreach mission is providing bicycles to people who need a mode of transportation to get to work. For the past month, Woolley G’s Bike and Fitness has refurbished bicycles and given them to Newgate Mission’s “Bike to Work” program. While Newgate primarily serves the city’s homeless community, the program is open to anyone needing a mode of transportation to get to work. The program is simple: People donate used but repairable bikes to Woolley G’s. Woolley G’s employees fix and donate them to Newgate. Newgate staffers then distribute them to people who need them. “We just thought that was a good opportunity,” said Gary Ford, a partner at Woolley G’s. “We get some that are in pretty good shape, and so it doesn’t take a lot to get them running.” In the past month, Woolley G’s employees have repaired five bikes for the program, Ford said. He dropped off two bikes at Newgate this past week. People who want to donate a bike to the program can bring it to Woolley G’s, 306 E Tyler St., each week from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Friday and 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday. People are encouraged to donate lightly used bikes rather than bikes that need serious, costly repairs. “If it’s not shifting well, not braking well, maybe needs some new tires or some new grips — that’s something that we can do inexpensively out of our own pocket,” he said. Woolley G’s is absorbing the cost of employee labor and minor repairs as part of the program, Ford said. Some community members are donating to Newgate to cover the cost of more significant repairs and to help repair bikes that people already have. Helping people who need a mode of transportation is rewarding, Ford said. “Not everybody can afford a car,” he said. “Bicycles are a cheap and expensive way to get around.” Jeanette Pleasant, an administrator at Newgate, said the program is helping people get to and from their jobs and government offices such as the Social Security Administration. “Most of them are off the street, homeless people,” she said. “We just try to help them and do as much as we can.” The program is open to anyone in need, not just Newgate clients, she said. “They can be somebody that just came in off the street or walked up here and needed a bike,” she said. “I just interview them, and if everything checks out for them, I give them a bike.” Newgate Mission is along Mobberly Avenue, where a bike lane was built as part of a “complete street” road renovation project. City leaders plan to build more bike lanes and sidewalks in the future to improve transportation for bicyclists and pedestrians alike. Those projects — and programs such as the Bike to Work program — will help people without cars get to work, grocery stores and more, Ford said. “If you’ve got a bike that’s kind of collecting dust in your garage, we’d love to get it in the hands of somebody that could use it,” he said. title: The Middleweight Adventure Bike That Delivers The GS Experience Without The GS Price - Top Speed
content: The GS badge has become shorthand for a serious adventure motorcycle, but that reputation comes with a premium price tag. BMW's F 900 GS combines a potent parallel-twin engine with off-road hardware and sophisticated rider aids, making it a natural benchmark for the middleweight ADV class. The question is how much of that performance you really need when your typical weekend involves winding back roads, the occasional gravel track, and a few hours in the saddle. There's a Japanese alternative that follows much of the same formula, including a 21-inch front wheel and spoked rims, while asking for considerably less of your wallet. The BMW F 900 GS makes a convincing case for its premium positioning with its 895cc parallel-twin being the heart of the package. It makes 105 horsepower at 8,500 rpm and 68.6 pound-feet of torque, which is plenty for a bike this size. It isn’t heavy, either. BMW lists the road-ready, fully fueled weight at about 482 pounds, helped along by a lightweight plastic fuel tank. The F 900 GS, however, carries a $14,495 MSRP plus $695 in destination, and that’s before you touch the options list or the accessory catalog. BMW also calls for premium fuel, so every fill-up costs a little more. Moreover, plenty of riders spend most of their time on pavement and gravel, so a chunk of that capability never gets used. You still pay for it, though. That gap is exactly where a Japanese parallel twin with a 21-inch front wheel and spoked rims wants to live, at a much friendlier price. That bike is the Suzuki V-Strom 800DE. It’s Suzuki’s off-road-focused middleweight adventure bike, built around the same 776cc parallel twin that powers the GSX-8S. Don’t mistake it for a budget stand-in, either. The 2026 model carries an MSRP of $11,799, plus $700 destination. The F 900 GS lists at $14,495 plus $695. The gap lands at $2,696, or about 18 percent of the BMW’s price. And the base model gets most of the hardware covered below: the 21-inch front wheel, long-travel suspension, and a full electronics package. Want to load it up? The V-Strom 800DE Adventure lists at $13,249. It adds 37-liter aluminum side cases, an accessory bar, a skid plate, and remote-adjustable rear suspension. Even then, it still costs about $1,200 less than a base F 900 GS. Under the tank sits a liquid-cooled, DOHC 776cc parallel twin. Bore and stroke are 84 x 70 mm, compression is 12.8:1, and a six-speed gearbox sends power to the rear wheel via chain. A 270-degree crank gives it a V-twin-like feel, while Suzuki’s Cross Balancer (two counterbalancers set diagonally) keeps vibration down and the engine compact. Suzuki says it deliberately favored smooth, low-rpm torque over chasing peak power. The Suzuki produces a claimed 83 horsepower at 8,500 rpm and 57.5 pound-feet of torque at 6,800 rpm. That leaves it approximately 22 horsepower and 11 pound-feet behind the BMW. This naturally makes the F 900 GS the quicker motorcycle. Its additional performance should be noticeable during hard acceleration, highway passing maneuvers, and spirited riding with luggage or a passenger. However, peak output doesn't tell the whole story. Reviews of the 800DE have praised its tractable power delivery and the way its Gravel traction-control setting allows controlled rear-wheel slip. Owner discussions similarly highlight its versatility on highways and dirt roads. For riders who value usable performance over outright acceleration, the Suzuki's engine makes a compelling case. Want something more road-focused? Both the F 900 GS and V-Strom 800DE enduro ADVs have adventure tourer alternatives. BMW offers the F 900 GS Adventure, which brings a larger fuel tank, improved wind protection, and an available Dynamic ESA electronic suspension. But tipping the scales at 542 pounds and starting at $15,195, it’s also the more expensive option. You don’t pay the same premium as the road-going V-Strom 800 base model, which starts at $10,294. This one features shorter suspension travel and basic spring preload adjustability, with cast wheels, the front being a 19-incher rather than a 21-incher. It also has a lower seat height, a street-focused windscreen, and non-switchable ABS. The Touring builds on this with a factory-installed topcase and handguards. If you prioritize road comfort over outright off-roading, the base V-Strom is a much better value than the F 900 GS Adventure. It's not as capable as the GS but will get the job done just fine. This is where the V-Strom really earns its keep. It rolls on a 21-inch front and a 17-inch rear spoked wheel, the same sizes as the BMW. Suspension travel is about 8.7 inches at both ends, with an inverted fork up front. BMW quotes 9.05 inches front and 8.46 inches rear for the F 900 GS, so it’s close to a wash. Ground clearance is 8.7 inches, the tallest in the V-Strom family. Suzuki even swept the muffler upward so it stays clear of all that long-travel suspension. That said, according to one reviewer, all that travel could mean a noticeable dive under hard braking that may take some getting used to. Weight is where you’ll notice a gap. The V-Strom’s curb weight is 507 pounds, while BMW lists 482 for the F 900 GS, fully fueled. Twenty-five pounds sounds small until you're picking it up out of a rut. Seat height tilts slightly in Suzuki’s favor. The V-Strom sits at 33.7 inches, against 34.2 inches for the standard F 900 GS. Half an inch might not sound like much, but it counts for shorter riders flat-footing at a stoplight. Suzuki covers the essentials well. The Suzuki Intelligent Ride System bundles three drive modes, traction control with a dedicated gravel setting, a rear-ABS-off option, and a standard bidirectional quick-shifter that leaves the clutch alone for most shifts. A five-inch color TFT display handles instrument duty. If you mostly want help on a dirt road, the Suzuki’s package covers the stuff that actually counts. Running costs tip toward Suzuki, too. Its 5.3-gallon tank also holds roughly 40 percent more than the F 900 GS’s 3.8 gallons, which helps when the next gas station sits a long way from the trailhead. The V-Strom’s weak spot is the warranty. Suzuki offers 12 months of limited coverage, versus BMW’s 36 months or 36,000 miles. But Suzuki bikes tend to outlast their European rivals, so that's the peace of mind you get with the V-Strom. Does the V-Strom 800DE give GS riders everything? Not quite. You give up some power, a few pounds, and warranty length. However, you keep the wheels, the travel, the clearance, and the electronics that matter off-road, and you keep $2,700 in your pocket. For plenty of weekend riders, that’s a trade worth making. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. title: The 5 Best ASUS Routers of 2026 - RTINGS.com
content: Few brands cast as wide a net in the world of Wi-Fi as ASUS. From their gamer-geared ROG and TUF lineups to the sleek ZenWiFi mesh family, the best router for you depends on what problem you're trying to solve. While this variety is a major plus for consumer choice, the sheer number of options available can certainly make finding the right one feel overwhelming. We've tested over 80 of the most popular routers, including over 15 ASUS routers (with more on the way). Below, you'll find our breakdown of the best ASUS routers on the market, chosen for their performance, features, and overall value. For more recommendations, check out our guides to the best gaming routers, the best long-range routers, and the best VPN routers. Since we started reviewing them in 2024, we've tested over 80 routers. We maintain complete editorial independence and impartiality by purchasing each router ourselves, which ensures we aren't testing specially selected review units. Rather than casually assessing performance by throwing on Netflix and seeing if it works, we rigorously evaluate each router on a standardized testing platform, providing you with all the data you need to compare different models. If you're after the absolute best ASUS router we've tested, look no further than the ASUS ZenWiFi BT10. This flagship Wi-Fi 7 mesh system is a fantastic choice if you live in a larger home, have multiple floors, or find that the coverage from a standalone router simply isn't cutting it. The two-pack variant we tested includes a companion node for added range, but the BT10 can also operate as a standalone if you don't need a multi-node mesh. Performance takes center stage here, with this router boasting the highest speed and range scores out of any ASUS device we've tested. Power users will be pleased with its solid mix of two 10Gbps ports, one 1Gbps port, and support for multi-WAN failover; it's ideal for ultra-fast fiber and Wi-Fi 7 devices, though its port selection is ultimately lighter than the generously equipped ASUS ROG Strix GS-BE18000. Specs aside, each node is sleek and low-profile, making it far easier to position around the home than some of the company's more angular designs from its 'gaming' entries. That convenience makes a difference, given that open placement is essential for achieving the best range and speed from a mesh system. Looking for more mesh router recommendations? We've got you covered. If you don't need a dedicated mesh or simply want a massive selection of Ethernet ports, we recommend the ASUS ROG Strix GS-BE18000 as the best ASUS router in the upper mid-range category. It's the best-performing Wi-Fi 7 standalone we've tested from the brand, making it an attractive option regardless of whether you plan to game. While its rugged styling obviously caters to gamers, the real draw comes from its combination of exceptional range, high-speed performance, and a stacked selection of multi-gigabit Ethernet ports that easily beat others in this class. Notably, this router includes Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) support to boost its 6GHz band's power and range, though this benefit only matters if you have Wi-Fi 6E or 7 devices (and live in a region that supports it). While this tri-band router's 2.5Gbps WAN port falls short of the ASUS ZenWiFi BT10's massive 10Gbps ceiling, it counters with a formidable array of seven 2.5Gbps LAN ports on the rear. If you're running multiple gaming consoles, PCs, or even a Network-Attached Storage (NAS) solution at home, you'd be hard-pressed to find a more cost-effective hub for a high-speed wired ecosystem (for example, the TP-Link Archer BE900 offers a similar number of high-speed ports, but costs nearly twice as much). Two of its ports are even designated "gaming ports"; in practice, this just means the router will supposedly prioritize traffic for whatever devices you connect to them. If the above options are outside your budget (or simply overpowered for your usage), we recommend the ASUS TUF Gaming BE9400 as one of the best ASUS routers at a mid-range price. Like our premium picks, this is still a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router with 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz bands, though it's best approached as a stellar general-use option rather than a niche gaming tool. While its tactical styling might not be to everyone's taste, it serves as a great example of what we found when looking at Wi-Fi latency and why gaming routers aren't inherently better: marketing aside, real-world performance comes down to what's under the hood. Thankfully, this router delivers exactly where it counts, all at a more competitive price. It maintains excellent speeds, strong coverage, and a great selection of multi-gigabit ports. While its chassis isn't particularly tailored to tight spaces, six adjustable antennas offer some flexibility in its positioning. This router delivers impressively low wireless latency, which is a meaningful advantage if you often game over Wi-Fi. Even so, the bottom line remains unchanged: Ethernet is king for competitive gaming. While you don't get the same seven-port selection as the ASUS ROG Strix GS-BE18000, this router still offers a respectable selection of three 2.5Gbps ports, leaving little room for complaint at this price. For a more budget-conscious entry into the latest wireless standard, we recommend the ASUS RT-BE92U as the best ASUS router at a lower mid-range price point. It sits on the pricier side of the lower-mid tier, but that's par for the course with ASUS's generally elevated price floor. Despite its positioning in the market, this router offers astonishingly high 6GHz peak speeds and respectable range for small to medium-sized homes. Its 10Gbps WAN/LAN port also provides an advantage over many similarly priced routers with slower Ethernet connections. While its standalone coverage leaves something to be desired, the model includes AiMesh support as a means to extend your range with compatible devices. An upright, angular design, coupled with four prominent antennas and a red racing stripe down the middle, gives this router a distinct "gamer" aesthetic, despite a lack of heavy marketing as such. Regardless, it's a highly capable mid-tier entry from ASUS and a cost-effective way to get your Wi-Fi 6E and 7 devices onto the 6GHz band (with unbeatable speeds for the price). If you want a straightforward, low-cost option and don't need cutting-edge Wi-Fi 7 technology, the ASUS RT-AX1800S is our top no-frills budget pick. As a dual-band Wi-Fi 6 router, it predates support for the faster 6GHz band. Even so, its hardware packs in plenty of utility for everyday users (learn more about the differences between Wi-Fi standards). Its defining strength lies in its value; a standard 1Gbps WAN port paired with a solid selection of four 1Gbps LAN ports makes this router more than sufficient for sub-gigabit internet plans. For a highly accessible price, it delivers reliable performance for basic web browsing, streaming, smart home tech, and simultaneous connections around the home. Naturally, that lower price tag means accepting a few trade-offs: the router's wireless range is limited, making it ill-suited to sprawling layouts, and a lack of multi-gigabit support caps its utility for any higher-speed internet plans. It isn't built to deliver the low latency or raw speeds required for power users or competitive gamers, but it's more than sufficient for everyday use and 4k streaming, even across multiple devices. That said, if your home is full of modern Wi-Fi 6E or 7 hardware (or if you just need a bit more headroom in the bandwidth department), stepping up to any of the recommendations above is well worth the investment. ASUS routers generally offer deep customization options through the ASUSWRT web interface and ASUS Router app. A big plus if you're the type to tinker, or simply want a higher degree of control over your network security. Unlike many competing router brands, ASUS doesn't lock common features behind a monthly subscription model. Features like parental controls, security tools, QoS, and VPN support are generally available without an ongoing fee. ASUS's higher-end routers and ZenWiFi mesh systems consistently deliver some of the strongest speed and range results we've seen from the brand. Many ASUS routers include a generous selection of multi-gigabit Ethernet ports. This is useful if you have wired devices such as a gaming PC or console, a NAS, a desktop workstation, or a home server. ASUS routers don't always deliver the best price-to-performance ratio; some competing brands offer similar or better performance for less, especially in the budget and mid-range categories. ASUS gives users plenty of control, but that depth can also make its software feel less intuitive at first. If you're after a plug-and-play setup with minimal configuration, you might find alternatives from other brands more appealing. TP-Link and ASUS both offer an extensive portfolio of routers, from budget models to powerful flagships. TP-Link is generally more competitive on performance per dollar in the mid-range space, while ASUS's deep network controls and configurability offer outstanding value to tinkerers, gamers, and enthusiasts. Crucially, the value of TP-Link's latest offerings has been undercut by subscription models that lock some security settings and advanced parental controls behind a monthly subscription. This is a practice that's becoming increasingly common in the industry, but ASUS has yet to adopt it. ASUS and eero take vastly different approaches to home networking. Eero's specialty is simplicity, with a clean, app-based ecosystem and polished user interface for effortless operation out of the box. ASUS offers far more control over your network through its app and web interface, with the ZenWiFi lineup being the closest direct competitor to eero's whole-home mesh solutions. Much like TP-Link, eero's advanced networking tools are locked behind a monthly subscription model, while ASUS includes comparable features at no additional cost. ASUS and NETGEAR are both prominent brands in the home networking space, but they appeal to different user needs. ASUS routers prioritize flexibility and granular control, with AiMesh technology that lets you mix and match compatible ASUS devices to build a mesh network. NETGEAR focuses on a more streamlined setup experience, but requires a recurring subscription for full access to security tools and parental control settings, in line with competitors. Additionally, some of NETGEAR's "Wi Fi 7" routers omit core generation features like Multi-Link Operation (MLO), making it important to verify specific hardware capabilities before buying. ASUS routers offer a mix of solid performance and flexible controls for users looking to get the most out of their internet plan. Features like mesh support, parental controls, and useful security tools are included across lineups and don't require a monthly subscription to access. While certain consumer lineups lean heavily into gaming-focused branding (such as ROG and TUF), the brand's consistent performance across a variety of price points makes ASUS a strong contender for most households, not just gamers. ZenWiFi: ASUS's flagship mesh series. These routers are generally sold in multi-pack systems and are designed to provide broader, more consistent whole-home coverage than a conventional standalone. Built around a simplistic app-based setup and a sleek, antenna-free aesthetic, ZenWiFi systems don't require a monthly subscription and also support AiMesh, so you can expand your network further with compatible devices. ROG (Republic of Gamers): The ROG lineup consists of ASUS's high-end standalone routers, marketed heavily towards gamers and enthusiasts. These models typically feature aggressive styling, a strong selection of multi-gigabit ports, and gaming-focused software features like traffic prioritization and dedicated 'gaming' ports. TUF Gaming: TUF Gaming routers are ASUS's more budget-focused gaming models, aiming to provide the same essential hardware features for power users at a more accessible price. TUF routers usually ship with a less expansive set of software tools, cutting out some extra features in favor of strong conventional performance and value. RT Series: ASUS's traditional RT lineup covers everything from entry-level home routers to premium standalone units. These routers cater to standard households, smart homes, and general users who want ASUS's signature network flexibility without gaming-specific branding. Most RT models still include ASUS's core software features, such as AiMesh support, parental controls, and more advanced networking settings. Goldman has three operating segments: Asset & Wealth Management, Global Banking & Markets, and Platform Solutions, with the latter including transaction banking and consumer partnerships. 10 Questions About Artificial Intelligence: Part 2 Artificial intelligence (AI) has been and remains one of the fastest-growing technology developments in history. Just a few years after becoming broadly known, AI represents a significant portion of the global economy and is now the preeminent focus among investors. Developments in AI have progressed and continue to unfold rapidly, and new revelations on one day - say, the release of Meta Platforms Inc.'s Muse model - can make preconceptions about AI seem out of date.  Based on input from clients, investors, industry experts, and our own analytic team, Argus has put together what we see as 10 current key and enduring questions about AI, along with our responses. We've broken these 10 questions into Parts 1, 2, and 3.  Part 2, presented below, addresses three key questions including risks that white-hot growth at the GPU makers might slow, key adjacencies benefiting from AI infrastructure build-outs, and a discussion of companies best and worst-positioned amid AI disruption. Following publication of Part 2, we will be publishing Parts 3. We welcome feedback from clients and will continue to refine our 10 questions about AI in real time in response to this exciting and ever-changing opportunity.  QUESTION 4: At the heart of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution are the graphics processing unit (GPU) developers, led by Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and followed by a host of others. What is the risk that these companies' white-hot growth slows or stops? ANSWER 4: AI infrastructure investment has broadened out from an initial focus on hyperscaler data centers to a broader set of customers, including enterprises, sovereigns, and neoclouds. Wider adoption is being driven by the much more diverse range of use cases driven by agentic AI. This broadening of the market has benefited the makers of GPUs, which represent the foundational piece in massive clusters required for model training, deep learning, and inference. Nvidia is the tentpole company of the AI revolution, initially repurposing its GPU gaming cards for early AI tasks. The company was also subject to fluctuations in the crypto market and consumer cycles in gaming demand. Nvidia's revenue declined 7% in fiscal 2020, rebounded to mid-50% annual growth in FY21 and FY22, and was flat in FY23 on softening in crypto and consumer end markets. After two years of triple-digit growth in FY24 and FY25, growth moderated to 6% in FY26 before reaccelerating to 87% in the January 2027 fiscal year. Although growth is on a path to 'moderate' to the 70% range in FY28, note that growth in dollars remains robust: rising from $216 billion in FY26 to an estimated $410 billion in FY27 and to $680 billion in FY28, according to the consensus. If not for supply constraints, according to CEO Jensen Huang, FY28 top-line growth would be meaningfully higher. Nvidia has teamed up with Wall Street giants (Apollo Global Management Inc., Blackrock Inc., Goldman Sachs Group Inc., and others) to raise $500 billion in capital for AI infrastructure. Nvidia anticipates multiple years of strong growth ahead. AMD is No. 2 in GPUs and is also benefiting as inference drives demand for industry standard servers (ISSs) using AMD's central processing units (CPUs). AMD generated $6.6 billion in revenue in 2010 but did not get back above that number until 2019. After three years of mid-double-digit growth in 2020-22, revenue declined in 2023 and grew 14% in 2024. Fueled by both its CPU and GPU franchises, growth accelerated to 34% in 2025 and is on a path to accelerate from 47% in 2026 to 73% in 2027. In dollar terms, AMD's revenue is forecast to rise from $35 billion in 2025 to $51 billion in 2026 and $88 billion in 2027. Companies including Broadcom Inc. and Marvell Technology Inc., which make application accelerators and XPUs (both of which are task-specific GPUs), are reporting similar growth trajectories as customer and market opportunities broaden. AI infrastructure spending grew about 60% annually to $320 billion in 2025, according to industry analysis firm IDC. AI infrastructure spending is on a path to exceed $1 trillion in 2029, the firm estimates. IDC noted that AI infrastructure investment is accelerating at a pace that signals a clear shift away from experimentation to a sustained, multiyear capital commitment cycle by end customers. Based on these and other forecasts and guidance from the major GPU providers, we expect GPU and related semiconductor growth to sustain and in many cases accelerate from high levels in coming years. QUESTION 5: What are some the key adjacencies that are benefiting from AI development? And which of these companies are best positioned to thrive? ANSWER 5: The initial gold-rush phase of AI was characterized by intense activity among hyperscalers to build massive GPU clusters and support infrastructure as they sought to develop and train their own large language models (LLMs). But this focus on AI data centers also represented one of the key bottlenecks in AI infrastructure. AI content, in the words of rock singer Meat Loaf, was 'all revved up with no place to go.' Late in 2024 and early in 2025, Argus noted that the AI revolution had primarily been focused within hyperscalers (major cloud service providers) and was concentrated in GPU compute at massive cloud data centers. Argus forecast that in coming years, the AI revolution would spread out from this initial concentration at hyperscalers to include customers in other categories including major enterprises, sovereigns, and neoclouds. We further forecast that the need to accommodate AI-generated data would trigger massive business growth at data storage and memory companies. And we forecast that the need to disseminate AI data to these new classes of customers would trigger massive business growth at data networking companies.  Those forecasts began to play out during 2025, as data storage and memory companies had huge business growth and were among the best stocks in the S&P 500. During 2026, data networking companies have reported strong double-digit growth rates, and their stocks are leading the Information Technology sector and broad market. The first phase of generative AI, dominated by the training of LLMs, is giving way to the age of agentic and physical AI, which requires much more compute-intensive inference in multimodal and frontier models. This is further contributing to AI-related data growth.  Technology segments benefiting from the need to deliver AI-as-a-system include data storage and memory, networking, and traditional enterprise infrastructure. In these segments, Argus has identified multiple companies best positioned to benefit from the broadening in AI demand. In the networking space, Argus favors optical-networking leader Ciena Corp., 'cloud titan' network provider Arista Networks Inc., and enterprise industry leader Cisco Systems Inc. as three companies well positioned to deliver AI services to customers. In the data storage and memory space, Argus favors Seagate Technology Holdings plc and Western Digital Corp., which form a duopoly in nearline hard disk drives for AI data centers; Sandisk Corp. in the nonvolatile memory space; and Micron Technology Inc., the leading U.S.-based provider of DRAM and NAND memory. Data storage systems providers including NetApp Inc. are subject to higher input costs for their solutions, but NetApp has driven revenue acceleration with successful cost pass-alongs and higher prices.  Dell Technologies Inc. is a good example of the fast-developing market opportunity in the legacy enterprise infrastructure space. As of mid-2026, Dell had thousands of customers for its AI servers and related IT infrastructure including storage arrays, industry standard servers, and networking gear. None of these customers included the major hyperscalers.  As of August 2026, Dell expected at least $74 billion in AI-optimized server revenue in FY27, almost triple the $25 billion in FY26. Dell's traditional x86-based ISS revenue grew more than 120% annually in the most recent quarter. In 1H27, Dell generated as much revenue from ISS and networking than it generated in any full prior year in company history.  Outside the Information Technology sector, industrial companies providing power, cooling, electrical, and related solutions are also experiencing extraordinary growth. Top beneficiaries include Caterpillar Inc., Emerson Electric Co., Honeywell International Inc., Rockwell Automation Inc., and others. As AI demand continues to broaden out, we expect strong and even accelerated growth for providers of the adjacent infrastructure enabling the AI revolution.   QUESTION 6: Which incumbents are most vulnerable to AI disruption? And which are best positioned to integrate AI defensively? ANSWER 6: The AI revolution has been so consistently strong and inclusive that it initially swept along much of the Information Technology sector. But as the AI revolution moves beyond year three, several significant developments have revealed risks to industry incumbents across the technology landscape. These developments primarily relate to AI displacement and the impact of soaring component costs in a supply-constrained environment. Fears of AI displacement have been mainly centered in the enterprise application software space. The trajectory of these fears is expressed in the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV). The software ETF hit an all-time closing high around 117 in September 2025. The release of certain highly capable frontier models, most notably Anthropic PBC's Claude Code, showed that many formerly proprietary software tasks could be done quickly and cheaply with AI. IGV declined gradually into year-end 2025 and then its decline accelerated in the new year, reaching bottom at a closing low of 74 in April 2026. IGV has since rebounded to a low-100s level, as software companies counter displacement fears by highlighting their proprietary products, deep customer engagements, and defense against 'weakest link' cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Component prices and particularly memory prices have soared due to voracious hyperscaler appetites for hardware to support infrastructure investment. Companies with high personal computer exposure such as HP Inc. report that memory is now up to 70% of the bill of materials cost of building a PC. In releasing its newest iPhone family in September 2026, Apple Inc. raised iPhone prices by approximately $100 per device and more for high-memory-content phones. These rising costs and the urgency to invest in AI are causing chief information officers to reshape their IT budgets in some cases away from long-standing customers.  International Business Machines Corp., which in April 2026 warned of a decline in 2Q26 infrastructure revenue, reported a steeper-than-expected demand decline in July 2026. Customers shifted purchases away from IBM's mainframe computers and its complementary transactional software stack. These customers redirected spending to ISS servers, a market in which IBM no longer competes, and data storage in order to secure supply-constrained IT hardware ahead of further price increases. IBM shares declined sharply on the 2Q26 revenue miss and are down 22% year-to-date. But the stock is up sharply from pre-AI days. IBM Watson playing Jeopardy against a past champion helped popularize the concept of AI years before ChatGPT. IBM, like the software companies and makers of AI PCs, should ultimately benefit from positioning within the AI ecosystem. We expect creative disruption to continue to challenge industry incumbents.  As to which companies are best positioned to integrate AI defensively, no company is in a position to sit on the sidelines and watch its competitors bring AI practices into their everyday operations and into customer interactions. Market sectors at the forefront of AI adoption, for both offensive and defensive reasons, include Healthcare, Information Technology, and Financial. Even in regulated sectors such as Utilities, which would seem to have less urgency to integrate AI into their operations, sector companies are adding smart meter technology and using AI to upgrade their internal operations. In short, nearly every company inside and outside of the AI ecosystem will need to integrate AI both offensively and defensively. Goldman Sachs is a storied financial institution, founded in 1869 and best known for its role as a leading global investment bank. The firm has a significant reach across global financial centers and has been the leading provider of global merger and acquisition advisory services, by revenue, for the past 20 years. Since the global financial crisis, Goldman has expanded its offerings into more predictable, fee-based businesses like asset and wealth management, which contributed roughly 30% of postprovision revenue at the end of 2025. The firm generates revenue from investment banking, global market making and trading, lending, asset management, wealth management, and a small and declining portfolio of consumer credit card loans. Was Monday a shot across the bow for semiconductor stocks prior to earnings season? If so, what do the sellers know? Or was it just the market setting the stage for a more-enticing buying opportunity ahead of third-quarter numbers? We don't know the answers to any of that, but we do know that the industry has not acted well following the failed breakout to recovery highs on October 6. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) have given back 7% in five days and recent breakouts from bullish inverse head-and-shoulders patterns have failed. In addition, many individual issues that appeared to be tracing out bullish bases for more than four months are now in question.
