title: Sölden Men’s GS 2026: Pinheiro Braathen Wins, Radamus Fourth - Ski Racing Media
content: Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, Marco Odermatt / GEPA pictures Three of the final four racers took the lead. The last man down the mountain won. Brazil’s Lucas Pinheiro Braathen delivered a commanding victory in Sunday’s Sölden men’s World Cup giant slalom, defeating Switzerland’s Loïc Meillard and Marco Odermatt in a thrilling opening to the 2026-27 season. The reigning Olympic and World Cup GS champion entered the second run with a 0.24-second advantage. What followed was an extraordinary battle on the Rettenbach glacier. American River Radamus held the leader’s chair deep into the final seven before three of the last four starters took turns moving into first place. Pinheiro Braathen eventually prevailed by 0.48 seconds, while just one hundredth separated the two Swiss podium finishers. The reverse-30 second run had already produced remarkable performances and several lead changes before the leading contenders prepared to challenge. Radamus, who had started the afternoon tied for 15th, remained the overall leader when only seven racers were left. His exceptional second run had forced the biggest names in giant slalom to chase his time. Henrik Kristoffersen, seventh after Run 1, couldn’t find the necessary speed and eventually finished 22nd. Germany’s Fabian Gratz also fell short of Radamus’ mark. Norway’s Atle Lie McGrath, fifth after the opening run, fell on the upper pitch and failed to finish. Odermatt, fourth after Run 1, delivered the seventh-fastest second run. The Swiss star finally ended Radamus’ extended stay in the leader’s chair. “I made a big step in the second run: I found the race gear and that’s the most important thing,” Odermatt told FIS. His third-place finish would ultimately become his 47th World Cup GS podium, establishing a Swiss record. It was an encouraging start after an offseason affected by injury. Austria’s Stefan Brennsteiner was next. Third after the opening run, Brennsteiner couldn’t match the pace. His second run ranked 22nd, dropping him to 11th overall and guaranteeing Odermatt a podium. The Swiss skier had finished the first run 0.31 seconds ahead of his teammate. He needed to protect that advantage to take the lead. Although Odermatt recorded a faster second run, Meillard delivered a strong finishing section and crossed just 0.01 seconds ahead. The result was especially satisfying for Meillard, who had never previously finished higher than fifth at Sölden. “Sölden and me haven’t been friends in the last few years so to start the season with a podium and some solid skiing feels good,” Meillard told FIS. The narrow margin over his teammate added another layer of satisfaction. “I had a few times when I was one-hundredth behind, so now it’s my turn to be in the front,” Meillard said. Odermatt recognized that the ultimate challenge remained the Brazilian who had dominated the opening run. “Lucas was too fast in the first run for the victory today,” he acknowledged afterward. Meillard had the lead. Odermatt was guaranteed third. Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, the reigning Olympic and World Cup GS champion, stood at the start knowing the entire race would be decided by his final run. Lucas Pinheiro Braathen stood at the start knowing he was the only racer who could deny Meillard victory. The 26-year-old Brazilian had already established himself as the world’s leading giant slalom racer, winning Olympic GS gold and the discipline’s World Cup crystal globe last season. Pinheiro Braathen had dominated the shortened first run, opening a 0.24-second advantage over Meillard and a 0.55-second lead over Odermatt. The same reduced course length was used for Run 2. Both runs had become intense sprints, with less accumulated fatigue but little opportunity to recover lost time. He increased his overall advantage through the opening and middle sections, reaching the final sector with 0.61 seconds in hand over Meillard. The Swiss skier had been particularly strong on the closing stretch, and Pinheiro Braathen surrendered some of his advantage approaching the finish. Pinheiro Braathen crossed 0.48 seconds clear, securing his fifth World Cup giant slalom victory and 12th podium in the discipline. His second-run time ranked 10th fastest. Combined with his exceptional opening performance, however, it was more than enough. Three of the final four racers had taken the lead. The final starter had won. Pinheiro Braathen acknowledged the expectations he carried into Sölden. “There was a lot of pressure on my shoulders today,” he said in his finish-area interview. “Pressure is privilege, and I was able to capitalize off of that.” The victory marked a remarkable contrast to the previous year’s Sölden opener, when Pinheiro Braathen failed to finish. This time, the Atomic and Oakley athlete arrived as the reigning Olympic champion and World Cup GS titleholder. “What a relief to be able to open the show in this way,” he said. Pinheiro Braathen explained that he had spent the offseason searching for new ways to improve following his Olympic gold and crystal globe. Those achievements brought confidence rather than hesitation. “I didn’t want to hesitate. I knew what I had in me,” he said. The Brazilian also thanked his family, team and supporters, recognizing their contribution to his latest victory. For the United States, River Radamus delivered one of the most impressive performances of the afternoon. The only Stifel U.S. Ski Team racer to qualify for the second run, Radamus finished the opening run tied for 15th, 1.15 seconds behind Pinheiro Braathen. “I was disappointed in my first run because I don’t think that I showed the skiing that I’ve been working towards,” Radamus said afterward. With some of the pressure lifted, the American attacked and produced a time of 51.99 seconds, the second fastest of the afternoon. Only Austria’s Raphael Haaser, who recorded 51.90, skied faster. “But the pressure was off a bit the second run, and I was able to connect some of the good turns that I’ve been working on,” Radamus said. “I’m happy with the progress we’re showing.” The American was particularly effective through the middle sector, where he posted the fastest time in the field. Against Haaser, who was leading when Radamus started, he built a 0.45-second advantage by the final intermediate split. Radamus lost 0.41 seconds of that cushion on the final stretch but crossed just 0.04 seconds ahead of the Austrian. One challenger after another failed to beat his combined time of 1:45.54. When the final seven racers prepared to start, Radamus was still leading. His performance had transformed the race, forcing the sport’s biggest stars to beat a time established by a racer who had finished the opening run in 15th. Eleven subsequent starters failed to displace him before Odermatt finally took the lead. Radamus ultimately finished fourth, climbing 11 positions and missing the podium by 0.33 seconds. Radamus offered valuable insight into why the second run produced so many impressive climbs. “The course was almost the exact same,” he said. “We were in the same grooves for a lot of it, so we knew what to expect.” The shortened course featured relatively open turns, allowing racers to maintain speed and attack. “It was very easy, very open. The snow was great,” Radamus explained. “You couldn’t afford to slow yourself down at all. You had to go at it.” That approach proved particularly effective for racers who had started the afternoon outside the leading group. Radamus also acknowledged that conditions changed between runs. The snow became more mixed, while visibility and wind remained considerations on the mountain. “The snow changed a bit between runs. It was like sort of a spring mix in the second run,” he said. Rather than dwell on the changing conditions, Radamus focused on making the most of them. “I tried to take advantage and make the most of it.” His result provided an outstanding start to the season. Radamus said he planned to remain in Europe for super-G training before returning to the United States to prepare for the upcoming World Cup races at Copper Mountain. Britain’s Freddy Carrick-Smith provided another of the afternoon’s memorable performances. The 19-year-old started the opening run wearing bib 46 and qualified for his first World Cup second run in a tie for 21st place. That achievement alone was significant for British alpine racing. His afternoon performance made the occasion even more memorable. Carrick-Smith produced the fifth-fastest second run, stopping the clock at 52.21 seconds. He climbed nine positions to finish 12th, earning his first World Cup points. “Yeah, it was amazing,” Carrick-Smith said afterward. “I guess I couldn’t have asked for much more out of my first run and second run.” The young Briton acknowledged that finishing his second run had been a priority. He held back slightly rather than risk losing the opportunity. Even so, his competitive time ranked among the day’s strongest performances. His breakthrough recalls fellow British racer Charlie Raposo’s World Cup giant slalom results at Kranjska Gora in March 2022. For a teenager competing against the world’s best, 12th place represents a significant career milestone. Carrick-Smith also spoke about representing a country with relatively few World Cup alpine competitors. “There’s not many GB skiers. It’s just good to be an influence, I guess.” Austria’s Raphael Haaser delivered the fastest second run of the competition, recording 51.90 seconds. Starting the afternoon in 20th, Haaser climbed 15 places to finish fifth, just 0.04 seconds behind Radamus. France’s Léo Anguenot also enjoyed a remarkable afternoon. The French racer temporarily occupied the leader’s chair before finishing ninth, improving 14 places from his first-run position. Norway’s Rasmus Bakkevig, the reigning Junior World GS champion, delivered another exceptional performance. Starting with bib 49, Bakkevig qualified 29th in the opening run. He then produced the fourth-fastest second run, taking an early lead and holding it through five subsequent challengers. He eventually finished 14th, climbing 15 positions. Six athletes moved up at least 10 places during the second run. Finland’s Eduard Hallberg earns the Ski Racing Media Bibbo Award, recognizing the greatest numerical improvement from original starting bib to final finishing position. Hallberg started with bib 55 and finished 16th, a difference of 39 positions. The Finn also recorded the fastest final sector of the second run, demonstrating impressive speed over the closing stretch. Bakkevig deserves recognition as well. The young Norwegian started bib 49 and finished 14th, a difference of 35 positions. Both performances illustrate the opportunities available to racers starting deep in the field. Switzerland left Sölden with two podium finishers, while Norway failed to place a racer in the top 10 despite qualifying six athletes for the second run. For a nation accustomed to success in men’s giant slalom, the absence of a Norwegian among the leaders was unusual. Kristoffersen dropped from seventh to 22nd, while Lie McGrath failed to finish. However, Norway’s younger athletes delivered encouraging performances. Eirik Hystad Solberg climbed from 13th to eighth, while Bakkevig’s remarkable second run demonstrated the potential of the next generation. Germany also showed improving depth in giant slalom. Three German racers qualified for the second run. Gratz finished sixth, Grammel climbed from 30th to 15th, and Alexander Schmid placed 21st. Norway led all nations with six second-run qualifiers. Austria and Switzerland each qualified four, while seven nations had just one racer advance. The 2026-27 World Cup giant slalom season opened with seven overall lead changes, remarkable climbs and an extraordinary battle among the final four racers. But when the competition reached its decisive moment, the reigning champion delivered. Pinheiro Braathen defeated two of Switzerland’s most accomplished racers and demonstrated that last season’s Olympic gold and crystal globe had not diminished his ambition. The Brazilian opened the season with victory, leaving his rivals with an immediate challenge: finding a way to beat the world’s leading giant slalom racer. Special thanks to Ski Racing Media journalist Darka Sefcik Starnova for her on-site reporting in Sölden and finish-area interviews, bringing the athletes’ voices and perspectives directly into this story. Darka Sefcik Starnova has loved ski racing since childhood, when she also competed in children’s categories. She founded United Ski Fans as a safe space for alpine ski racing enthusiasts, both online and at the races. Through this project, she shares engaging content from the world of fandom, fan clubs, and grandstand fun — simply for the joy of it. Darka is especially dedicated to the fan clubs of Petra Vlhová and Lucas Pinheiro Braathen. She believes alpine skiing is a sport of love, where fans treat each other with kindness and many athletes serve as role models for the younger generation. In her professional life, Darka works in education, where she values healthy and positive role models just as strongly. Ski Racing Media is the leading international media company in alpine skiing, providing industry expertise, storytelling, and education.

title: The Cheapest Adventure Bikes With More Than 100 Horsepower - HotCars
content: Today, the adventure bike market is almost as diverse as the industry itself, with a wide range of bikes that will appeal to pretty much every kind of rider. While there is a growing contingent of riders gravitating towards lighter, more off-road oriented machines, there are still several great adventure-tourers on the market that will appeal to those looking for something more comfortable and powerful. All these bikes offer a semblance of off-road potential, but bigger, more powerful engines most certainly weigh more, and once you reach a certain weight class, serious off-roading is more or less off the table. Realistically speaking, most riders are not buying an ADV for that purpose, they will primarily be using them for long distance travel, and that is where all these bikes shine. Offering more comfort and features than some dedicated touring bikes. Most modern bikes share engines. For the sake of variety, we limited it to one model per platform. We are still struggling to unpack exactly how MV Agusta is able to price the Enduro Veloce like this for the US market. We can only assume that they are betting on selling enough of them to make up for whatever profit is lost on each model. These bikes come fully equipped with all the adventure-touring toys, from those hard cases to IMU-backed electronics. In an effort to win back some semblance of consumer confidence, these bikes come with a 5-year warranty ... if MV will still be around for that long. It is worth remembering that this is a company that simply rolls from one financial crisis to another. Unlike MV, who seem determined to live out every conceivable Italian cliché known to man, Ducati has long since found a way to build more reliable bikes without losing their identity. One of the more recent reliability-centered decisions was ditching desmodromic valves for certain models, and the DesertX is one of them. While desmo has its place in high-performance models, conventional variable valve timing is most certainly a better, more practical choice for this middleweight ADV. A third Italian bike in as many entries may leave some ADV enthusiasts scratching their heads, but the Stelvio’s unconventional transverse V-twin delivers an impressive 115 horsepower. Piaggio’s flagship ADV continues to get upstaged by the Aprilia Tuareg 660, though, and it is pretty easy to see the appeal of the lighter “brother from another mother.” For those looking for a more comfortable long distance tourer, the Stelvio is most certainly worth the extra outlay. Suzuki has a knack for making the most out of older engines and the big V-Strom is no exception. This twin can trace its roots all the way back to the infamous TL1000S (and TL1000R sport bike). While it has been reworked to better suit the ADV, it is still a fun, tractable engine that belies the rather uninspiring design of the bike. At least the V-Strom won’t suddenly lose its rear end like the old TL1000S! For all those KTM enthusiasts screaming at the screen, the Norden 901 is cheaper, and an objectively better looking bike. It certainly lacks the off-road capability of the 890 Adventure R (which really is remarkable for its size) but if that is really what you are after, then it might actually be worth considering the new 690 Rally, which is even cheaper than the Norden, but not even in the same conversation when it comes to long-distance comfort. When compared to the aforementioned V-Strom 1050, we have always found the Africa Twin surprisingly affordable. The base model is more off-road oriented, but at the end of the day, this is still a 500 pound motorcycle, and off-road, it will handle like a 500 pound motorcycle. Along with being surprisingly affordable, it is also surprisingly comfortable. What is not surprising at all is the fact that it is as reliable as any Honda product, so peace of mind is simply part of the deal. The base model Tiger 900 is more street oriented than any of the other 900s, and while you still reserve the right to go off-road with more confidence than the average street bike, it is more of a tourer. It is an exceptionally comfortable bike, and like most triples, it offers the best of both worlds in terms of performance, with the grunt of a twin and high RPM performance of an inline-four. Also, like most triples, you will get some vibrations through the bars at highway speed. It will bother some, and won’t fuss others. A test ride is essential! Upon first inspection, the F 900 GS looks like a bit of a bargain. The base model already comes with an Akrapovič exhaust, and it offers the most off-road potential out of all these 100-ish horsepower ADVs (the DesertX might have something to say about this), but with BMW there is always a “but.” Even the paint you see in this photo will cost extra, and so will several other features that really shouldn’t be optional at this price point. China has arrived to the big bore ADV party in the most Italian way possible. While Moto Morini bikes are all built in China, they are also designed in Italy, and it shows, because the X-Cape family are among the best looking adventure bikes on the market. This V-twin was also developed in Italy (albeit some two decades ago) before the company was absorbed by its Chinese parent, and makes a healthy 129 horsepower. The Ibex 950’s arrival is unusually quiet compared to the excitement that surrounded the lightweight 450. It features an uprated version of the KTM LC8c parallel twin which now makes 112 horsepower. Only time will tell if it still has the same appetite for cams as the version found in the aforementioned Norden, but if CFMoto has solved that problem, this might be the ADV deal of the year. If there was any suggestion that Lucas Pinheiro Braathen (BRA/Atomic) would suffer a letdown this season after his extraordinary success earlier this year, those fears have been put to rest at the first time of asking. The Brazilian won the season-opening Giant Slalom race in Sölden on Sunday, marking his fourth straight elite GS victory, including his Olympic triumph and the late-season wins that propelled him to the 2026 Crystal Globe. Leading after the first run, Pinheiro Braathen skied aggressively but calmly in the second run to cruise to a deserved victory by nearly half a second over Loïc Meillard (SUI/Rossignol, +0.48s) and Marco Odermatt (SUI/Stöckli, +0.49s). "There was a lot of pressure on my shoulders today," Pinheiro Braathen said, referencing the beginning of his title defense and the highly-anticipated resumption of his rivalry with former GS king Odermatt. "But pressure is privilege and I was able to capitalize on that. What a relief to be able to open the show in this way." After returning to the tour two years ago with Brazil following a year in retirement after his early career with Norway, the 26-year-old has methodically ticked off a series of firsts for the nation he now represents: first World Cup win, first Winter Olympic medal (and gold at that), first Crystal Globe. Having reached those dizzying heights in such a short time, the philosophical Pinheiro Braathen put a lot of thought over the off-season into what would come next. "I've been searching for new curiosities, new paths to evolve from last year's Olympic gold and the Globe," he said. "We're headed towards new goals, new objectives." Yet he produced the same brilliant skiing that has repeatedly propeled him to the top of the podium in recent times. When he crossed the finish line in first place, he emphatically yelled "Vamos!" into the camera. "Even already from the second half of last season, I was able to bring that freedom that came with being able to accomplish those results, and bring that spirit into the very first race (on Sunday)," he said. "I didn't want to hesitate, I knew what I had in me, and I'm so, so proud to put it out there." On a bumpy, windy course from the reserve state gate that reduced each run to under a minute, there was no room for errors or hesitation even as the skiers were trying to find the snow under their feet in their first race of the season. While Pinheiro Braathen mastered the conditions the best, the Swiss pair of Meillard and Odermatt showed they are not far from the top of their game, even at this early stage of the season. Meillard, in particular, tends to start slowly and work his way into the season, and he had never finished higher than fifth on the Rettenbach glacier before Sunday. "Sölden and me haven't been friends in the last few years so to start the season with a podium and some solid skiing feels good," he said. As the second-last skier on the mountain, he trailed provisional leader Odermatt at the final intermediate split, but used a scintillating closeout to overtake his teammate by the barest of margins in ski racing: one-hundredth of a second. "I had a few times when I was one-hundredth behind, so now it's my turn to be in the front," Meillard said. "I guess next race, it's him again, and that's the beauty of the sport." Odermatt, the four-time Giant Slalom title winner who lost his Olympic gold and his Crystal Globe to Pinheiro Braathen last season, was satisfied with third after having his pre-season affected by injury. "To start the season with a podium is always nice," he said. "I made a big step in the second run: I found the race gear and that's the most important thing." Odermatt's 47th World Cup Giant Slalom podium moved him ahead of Michael Von Gruenigen (SUI) and Vreni Schneider (SUI) for the most all-time among Swiss racers, and that podium was about the most he could have hoped for on this day. "Lucas was too fast in the first run for the victory today," Odermatt admitted. For Pinheiro Braathen, it was his second victory in Sölden after he triumphed in 2020 while racing for Norway, and the personal journey he has undertaken between those wins was not lost on him. "It's amazing to look back at being able to be the youngest winner here and to come and do it again," he said. "That's something very special for me. That very day here, when I was 20 years old, that changed my life." Six years later, racing under a different flag and with new perspectives on skiing and life, it all came together for the Brazilian on Sunday. "I was just able to be me, I was able to be so connected with myself, and it felt so fun to ski that second run," he said. "I knew that this was how I was supposed to feel. And that's the feeling that I chase every single day.

title: Sölden Men’s GS 2026: Pinheiro Braathen Leads Run 1 - Ski Racing Media
content: Lucas Pinheiro Braathen returned to Sölden on Sunday, Oct. 25, and delivered the fastest first run of the men’s 2026-27 Alpine World Cup opener. Behind him, seven racers starting bib 31 or higher fought their way into the second run, transforming the battle for qualification. A year after failing to finish the opening giant slalom on the Rettenbach glacier, the Brazilian Olympic champion and reigning World Cup GS titleholder showed exactly why he enters the new season as the skier to beat. Racing on Atomic skis and wearing Oakley eyewear, Pinheiro Braathen clocked 52.40 seconds. Switzerland’s Loïc Meillard finished just 0.24 seconds behind, while Austria’s Stefan Brennsteiner took third at +0.49. Defending Sölden champion Marco Odermatt sits fourth, 0.55 behind the leader, setting up an intriguing second-run battle. Strong winds forced organizers to start at the top of the steep pitch, shortening the first run to about 53 seconds. Overcast skies reduced visibility, and organizers removed the usual banner above the finish due to wind concerns. U.S.-born Norwegian Atle Lie McGrath, racing on HEAD skis, became the first man to start a World Cup race in the new season. Austrian Stefan Brennsteiner quickly set a faster benchmark before his teammate, Marco Schwarz, disappointed the home crowd with an early mistake that ended his run. Schwartz said, “Conditions are great, no issue, good work. I just wanted to be in a very straight line and it didn’t work.” Starting fourth, the Brazilian delivered the fastest middle sector and established a lead that survived all 69 starters. Meillard offered the closest challenge. After struggling to find his best form early last season, the Swiss star produced an encouraging performance. He matched the fastest opening-sector time but surrendered most of his 0.24-second deficit near the finish. Odermatt, racing on Stöckli skis and Salomon boots, remained within striking distance but lost 0.29 seconds in the middle sector alone. Henrik Kristoffersen provided another revealing contrast. The Norwegian matched the fastest opening split but lost 0.58 seconds in the final sector, leaving him seventh. The opening group established the early contenders, but improving visibility soon created opportunities for the racers starting behind them. As the light improved, several later starters demonstrated that the early leaders were not beyond reach. Germany’s Fabian Gratz, wearing bib 10, moved into sixth. Then Italy’s Giovanni Borsotti delivered one of the morning’s strongest performances, charging into eighth from bib 29, just 0.79 seconds behind Pinheiro Braathen. Germany’s Alexander Schmid followed from bib 27, finishing ninth at +0.84. France’s Thibaut Favrot, starting 21st, claimed 10th after producing a final sector just 0.01 seconds slower than the leader. Croatia’s Filip Zubčić also offered an encouraging sign. After a difficult season and a switch to Nordica skis and Marker bindings, the proven GS contender finished 12th, only 0.98 seconds behind. Belgium’s Sam Maes, who trains with the Stifel U.S. Ski Team and races on Völkl skis, finished 11th at +0.92. River Radamus was the lone American to qualify, finishing tied for 15th, 1.15 seconds behind Pinheiro Braathen. The Stifel U.S. Ski Team racer initially crossed in 10th but gradually slipped as later starters delivered faster performances. Radamus has demonstrated the ability to produce exceptionally fast individual runs, leaving him an opportunity to attack in the afternoon. Great Britain’s 19-year-old Freddy Carrick-Smith delivered an even more dramatic performance. Starting bib 46, the young British racer charged into a tie for 21st, just 1.37 seconds behind the leader. He finished 25 positions ahead of his starting number, securing a rare World Cup giant slalom second run for Britain. The achievement recalls Charlie Raposo’s performance at Kranjska Gora in March 2022, when the British racer advanced to the second run and finished 27th. No Canadian, Japanese or South Korean racers qualified. The final starting group delivered one of the morning’s biggest surprises. With only one of the opening 30 racers failing to finish, opportunities appeared limited for those starting farther back. Yet seven racers wearing bib 31 or higher qualified for the second run, displacing several established competitors. Improving visibility helped create opportunities, but these athletes still needed exceptional execution to capitalize. Fastest high-bib qualifier: Sandvik, who finished 18th from bib 32. Highest bib to qualify: Hallberg, who started 55th and finished 26th. Biggest improvement: Hallberg also made the largest move, gaining 29 positions relative to his starting number. Italy’s Franzoni provided another remarkable highlight. Despite losing a full second in the middle sector, he produced the fastest final sector of the entire field, beating Pinheiro Braathen’s split by 0.13 seconds. The battle for qualification proved unforgiving. Ryder Sarchett of the Stifel U.S. Ski Team initially moved into 27th from bib 34, but later finishers pushed him outside the top 30. Seven successful high-bib qualifiers demonstrated the depth of the field and ensured that the opening race delivered drama well beyond the fight for the lead. The fastest 30 return in reverse order, with Pinheiro Braathen starting last. The Brazilian holds the advantage, but Meillard, Brennsteiner and Odermatt remain close enough to challenge. After a first run filled with surprises, the fight for the season’s opening World Cup victory is far from decided. title: Suns 131-122 Warriors (Oct 24, 2026) Game Recap - ESPN
content: PHOENIX -- — Devin Booker scored 43 points, Miles Bridges added 16 and the Phoenix Suns won their home opener for the fifth straight season by beating the short-handed Golden State Warriors 131-122 on Saturday night. The Warriors — who were playing for the third time in four days — fell to 0-3 for the first time in 19 years while resting several key players, including Stephen Curry (right knee), Brandin Podziemski (low back), Draymond Green (low back) and Al Horford (low back). Booker scored 17 points in the third quarter and Jordan Goodwin hit a 3-pointer just before the buzzer to give the Suns a 102-92 lead entering the fourth. The Warriors hung around for a few more minutes, but the Suns eventually pulled away and Luke Kennard hit a 3 to extend the lead to 117-102 with six minutes left. Kennard finished with 11 points, hitting 3 of 5 from 3-point range, which is exactly what the team expected when they signed him in the offseason. Dillon Brooks had 15 points and five assists. The Suns were coming off an embarrassing 124-83 road loss in the season opener to the Trail Blazers. They struggled in the opening quarter of Saturday's game, too, making just 1 of 12 shots from 3-point range. But the shots finally started to fall and it was Booker who led the way. The five-time All-Star made 17 of 25 from the field and added seven assists and seven rebounds. Golden State was led by rookie Yaxel Lendeborg, who scored a season-high 26 points and made six 3-pointers. De'Anthony Melton added 25 points on 8 of 13 shooting. Booker scored 19 points in the first half, leading the Suns to a 57-54 halftime lead. Lendeborg had 13 for the Warriors. Suns: At Oklahoma City on Monday night.
